recipes.name: Belgian Waffles
ingredients_raw: 0.25 cup warm milk (110 degrees F/45 degrees C)
2.75 cups warm milk (110 degrees F/45 degrees C)
0.75 cup butter, melted and cooled to lukewarm

steps.text: In a small bowl, dissolve yeast in 1/4 cup warm milk. Let stand until creamy, about 10 minutes.

In a large bowl, whisk together the egg yolks, 1/4 cup of the warm milk and the melted butter. Stir in the yeast mixture, sugar, salt and vanilla. Stir in the remaining 2 1/2 cups milk alternately with the flour, ending with the flour. Beat the egg whites until they form soft peaks; fold into the batter. Cover the bowl tightly with plastic wrap. Let rise in a warm place until doubled in volume, about 1 hour.

Preheat the waffle iron. Brush with oil and spoon about 1/2 cup (or as recommended by manufacturer) onto center of iron. Close the lid and bake until it stops steaming and the waffle is golden brown. Serve immediately or keep warm in 200 degree oven.

raw_recipe.headline: Belgian Waffles
raw_recipe.description: The yeast in these eggy waffles makes for exceptionally deep pockets, perfect for capturing melting butter and syrups.

review.reviewBody: I loved this recipe! True belgian waffles are a yeast batter, and this one is very genuine. My only gripe is that it makes a lot of dishes (yeast, butter, milk, mixing bowl, egg whites). I subbed one cup of whole wheat flour with no noticeable effect on texture; next time I'll do two cups each whole wheat and white. I'm not sure why the egg whites are whipped and folded in separately. The loft comes from yeast, and by the time the dough is risen surely the egg whites will have deflated. I did it anyway. This batter does not actually double in volume as the recipe states; it's risen when it is bubbly and there is a yeast smell. As an experiment, immediately when I finished the batter I put one waffle's worth in the fridge, to see if I could do a slow cold rise that would allow the batter to be made ahead. I made the waffle the next day, almost 24 hours later, and it was sensational. I think it was even better than the waffles made the first day, yeastier and more complex in flavor. So I am happy to report the batter can be made ahead; no need to wait an hour in the morning to have your waffles. To make an easy, delicious, and healthy fruit sauce, dump a bag of frozen berries into a saucepan and keep over medium heat while you cook the waffles. Let boil until they "dissolve" into sauce. Adjust taste with sugar (usu only a tbsp is needed for 1 lb berries) and lemon juice (usu 1.5 tsp). The yield for my 7" round belgian waffle maker was about 10 waffles.

FINALLY a recipe worthy of a five star rating! I have made these waffles several times. For time purposes, I prefer preparing the batter the night before versus the morning of. However, I haven't noticed a distinct difference in the taste either way - the waffles are amazingly delicious! I whip the egg whites first, since I use my KitchenAid stand mixer and don't have an extra mixing bowl; then set the egg whites aside. Proofed the yeast in the mixing bowl (add a tsp of sugar with the yeast to proof it properly - the yeast mixture should be frothy after 10 minutes). Then I add the egg yolks, etc.. directly to the yeast. Be sure the milk and butter aren't too hot, otherwise it will kill the yeast - should be no more than 115°F. The batter should relatively double in size. I used a 7" Belgian Waffle iron and ended up with 9 waffles (about 1 scant cup of batter per waffle). A regular waffle iron will produce many more waffles due to difference of size/shape. These waffles are crispy outside and soft inside. If you are accustomed to "Belgian Waffle" mix from a box, these will taste much different, because they are made from a yeast batter - but true Belgian Waffles are made with yeast. We top ours with butter, maple syrup, strawberries and whipped cream, YUM! The waffles freeze well - just be sure to reheat them in the oven for about 10 minutes at 350-375°F to keep the crispness.

Really good! Woke up with a desire for mimosas and Belgian waffles and went for it. I used rapid rise yeast but it still had to sit for at least an hour before it seemed like it had risen. It definitely didn't "double" but it was bubbly, airy looking, and yeasty smelling and had visibly risen. I followed the directions exactly and we loved them. Super light and fluffy on the inside and crunchy on the outside. Make sure you carefully watch your temperatures for your milk and do not pack the flour! SCOOP flour into measuring cup with a spoon, then level off with a knife. I suspect that is why some people are ending up with dense waffles. I have just a regular Black & Decker circular waffle iron, I'd guess 7"? It made 9 waffles. I think it would have made 8 if they were perfectly measured, but the first one I made I only used about 1/2c batter and so it was a bit small. The rest I used about a scant cup. Love them, either we are having chicken & waffles for dinner or I'll freeze them individually with the food saver for quick breakfast. It is a lot of effort, I may double next time. Thanks!

All in all, this is an excellent recipe, but I reduced the rating to 4 stars only because it doesn't have to be quite so labor intensive or use so many bowls. 

Changes that I made were primarily because I made the batter the night before , and I had only 2 cups of milk on hand. I used my Kitchenaid mixer, but this method could also be used for a hand electric mixer. 

In a medium bowl, I melted the butter in the microwave and then added the 2 cups of milk that I had and 1 cup of water. This cooled the butter and warmed the milk. For the additional cup of milk, I used powdered buttermilk that was added to the dry ingredients. I separated the eggs, adding the yolks to the butter/milk mixture, and put the whites in a small bowl. The milk, egg yolks and butter were mixed together to combine. 

All of the dry ingredients were put into the Kitchenaid mixer bowl (flour, sugar, salt, buttermilk powder, and 1 1/2 tsp. instant yeast. (If you make this in one day, use 1 3/4 tsp. instant yeast) and mixed with the beater tool. Then I added the milk, butter, egg yolk mix, and combined using the beater tool. While this was mixing, I used a hand mixer to beat the egg whites until they peaked. 

Then I folded the egg whites into the batter, covered the bowl, and let it sit on the counter for 1/'2 hour before I put it into the refrigerator. Since we had the waffles for dinner, i took the batter out of the frig about an hour before I planned to bake them so the batter could warm and raise.

I made this recipe the night before and placed it in the fridge overnight for the longer rise. It was ready to go first thing in the morning. The 1/2 cup was just right for each waffle size. 

I would suggest using a dough hook or hand mixer when going back and forth between the milk and flour additions and use a large bowl as it states or else this will slosh everywhere. I used a large metal mixing bowl and it was just slightly over the brim after the overnight rise. 

This recipe made 14 waffles for me and I let them cool, turning them over to allow the heat to escape and firm up, before putting them in a freezer plastic bag. I'm able to have breakfast ready by placing them in the toaster.

The best homemade waffles we've ever made! Light and fluffy, mildly sweet so whatever toppings you use can shine through. Making the batter is pretty involved, lots of bowls to wash, but worth it. Be sure to use a very large bowl for rising. Mine only had a third left open to rise and our batter overflowed after about 40 minutes. I use my oven on 100 degrees to proof any yeast recipes, that gave a very good rise with this one. We use a deep Belgian style iron. I'm going to try making batter the night before next time and refrigerate, and giving it a little time to warm up and re-rise in the morning next time, as some of the reviews have suggested.

I have a recipe from my Belgian cousin. It islighter for sure. I substituted 1/2 cup club soda for the liquid Nd added another package of yeast. All this provides a lighter waffle. The vanilla and butter add flavor to this rendition. It was a good comprise.

I got my waffle-loving guy a Cuisinart WAF-F20 Double Belgian Waffle Maker for his birthday. I tried Arrowhead Mills and Whole Foods mixes but they were not up to snuff. On New Year's Day, I had time to make Bobbi Jo's yeasted waffle recipe and we both loved it.

I made a couple of substitutions because I didn't have milk or all-purpose flour:
 - Flour: King Arthur unbleached white bread flour
 - Milk: for the yeast 1/8 c each of half an half and unsweetened almond milk; for the rest: 1/2 c half and half and almond milk for the rest.

This recipe deserves a spotlight. The best waffles I've had in my life- I make it for all 8 kids and many times a child splits one. These are the fluffiest things! . My trick to keeping everything warm is to use glass bowls and preheat them in the microwave. I reuse my kitchen made mixing bowl after mixing the batter to beat the egg white and then combine them in a large warm glass bowl. Then I stick the proofing mixture in the cold oven with a cup of boiling water on the side for heat and humidity. Great Sunday breakfast! I've made this recipe no less than 50 times now and if you follow the instructions it comes out exactly like the picture.

This was great. Turned out very light and crisp, I’ll certainly do this one again and saved the recipe. Where I see people having trouble with this would be paying attention to the temperatures so you keep the yeast happy and productive. 105-110 for your milk to proof the yeast, you have to proof the yeast. 105-110 for the rest of the dairy, warm it up near the end of the proofing. To cold and the little yeasties won’t wake up, to hot they die. Let your eggs sit out for a bit to come to room temp. I microwave my big Pyrex bowl to warm it up a bit because it would be like jumping in a cold pool after being in a sauna for the yeast, keep them cozy. The big key to this recipes success is happy yeast. By the end of an hour ferment this batter was close to doming my big bowl. Everyone was digging these waffles as they were for a special occasion, breakfast for dinner.
I made these waffles vegan by using vegan margarine, arrowroot powder for eggs, and almond milk. I've made them probably 50 times now.

Honestly, this is an amazing recipe that I love to use! I recently made it gluten-free for dietary reasons, and it tastes just as great. Some adjustments I made to combat the tendency for gluten-free waffles to become gritty, dry, dense, or fall apart: -Switched out regular flour for Bob’s Red Mill GF blend (it’s a 1:1 blend and my favorite GF flour). -Used only 1–2 Tbsp of sugar (My family isn’t big on sweet dishes, and before we made the recipe gluten-free, we didn’t use any sugar at all so I added it only to help the waffles become crispier) -Added an extra 1/2 tsp of vanilla. -Added 2–4 Tbsp of warm milk to the batter (be careful with 4 Tbsp, as it can make the batter slightly runny) -Added 1 1/2 Tbsp of butter. -Added an extra 1/2 tsp of salt. Most importantly, I warmed the eggs beforehand, which is a helpful trick in many gluten-free recipes to ensure smooth mixing. One small note: I ran out of milk and used heavy cream instead. It worked fine, but it made the final dish more bitter than usual Overall, this recipe is fantastic, adaptable, and perfect for an easy-to-make breakfast that stores well.
Light a fluffy waffles 🧇 that are a family favorite.
We made a couple of tweaks by using brown butter and homemade vanilla bean paste and they are to die for!
Amazing waffles!! So tasty and they kept their shape! Will be making it again for sure!
I’ve been using this recipe for a more than 10 years and we all love it! No changes!
This is the best waffle recipe I have to date.

I've made this recipe for years. Makes about 10 round waffles. I put them in the freezer on a baking sheet that is lines with a silicone mat and freeze them and later transfer them to ziplock freezer bags. My son loves to toast them in the toaster oven. Crisp and yummy!!!! Thank you for this recipe!
Great waffle could be crispier but my son and I enjoyed them very much
